newsitem.title: PERU: Peru extends "faceless" courts for one year.
newsitem.headline: Peru extends "faceless" courts for one year.

text.p: Congress voted late on Thursday to extend for one year Peru's controversial "faceless" court system that has jailed thousands of guerrillas but also put hundreds of innocents behind bars.
The vote was 61-19 to prolong the secret tribunals, which have been a key component of official anti-guerrilla strategy since 1992 but have outraged human rights groups.

"The faceless judges must continue their functions," said Gilbero Siura, a legislator from the ruling New Majority-Change 90 party. "The achievements already obtained in judging and sentencing these criminals are positive since they have pacified the country 95 percent."

Under previous legislation, the tribunals, whose anonymous judges often wear hoods or sit behind one-way screens, were due to end their functions on Oct. 15. But a series of top officials in President Alberto Fujimori's administration had publicly backed extending the system, arguing it was necessary to combat the still latent threat from communist guerrillas.

In a long and heated debate, opposition legislators in the single-chamber Congress, where the government controls 70 of the 120 seats, condemned the courts as a mockery of justice. "A faceless judge does whatever he wants. Faceless judges are a negation of justice," said Henry Pease of the Union For Peru party (UPP).

"Even if we accept that the faceless trials have contributed to eliminate the subversive phenomenon, their extension could provoke new injustices like the 400 cases that are currently being considered by a special government committee," said Aldo Estrada Choque, also of UPP.

The government, which has since 1995 released nearly 250 prisoners falsely convicted of terrorism, admits up to 400 more wrongly accused inmates may be behind bars and has named a special panel to examine their cases and recommend pardons.

Human rights groups say the number is nearer 1,000, with most of the innocent prisoners convicted by secret courts on flimsy evidence, often obtained by torture, and without the chance of a fair trial.

Some of the first 31 prisoners to be pardoned under recommendations of the government committee told last week how they were brutally forced to sign confessions or were convicted on the uncorroborated word of one informer.
Arguing that normal courts were failing to convict terrorists through incompetence, corruption or fear, Fujimori first introduced the faceless courts in 1992 to combat escalating guerrilla violence.

The Maoist Shining Path guerrilla group has been greatly weakened since the 1992 capture of its leader Abimael Guzman but has been flexing its muscles this year with a series of car-boinations and clashes with security forces.
Conflicts caused by Shining Path and the smaller Tupac Amaru Reionary Movement (MRTA) have caused about 30,000 deaths and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
